# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

values.value: Why MCP is awesome
The Model Context Protocol gives AI assistants one standard, auditable way to reach the systems we already run.

value.markup:
Every integration used to be a bespoke adapter. Each assistant, each tool and each CMS needed its own glue code, its own auth story and its own idea of what a request looks like.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) replaces that patchwork with one contract. A server exposes capabilities as named tools with typed inputs. A client discovers them and calls them. That is the whole idea, and it is a good one.

values.value: Photo by Alexandre Debiève on Unsplash

value.markup:
Why it is awesome: it is boring in the right ways. The tools are declared with schemas, so mistakes are caught at the boundary. The same server works for any MCP client, and because the interface is explicit you can read exactly what an agent is allowed to do.

In this project, the Umbraco MCP server lets an agent model document types, create content and manage media without a single click in the back office.

values.value: Why MCP is awesome, part 2
Content without the clicking: how an MCP server turns a CMS into something an agent can build with.

value.markup:
In part one we covered the idea. Here is what it feels like in practice.

Modelling content is a sequence of small, checkable steps: create an element type, move it into the right folder, create the data type it needs, then read it back to confirm it took. Each step is a tool call with a clear result.

values.value: Photo by Vardan Papikyan on Unsplash

value.markup:
The part I like most is the feedback loop. When a block payload is wrong it fails quietly, so the habit is to read structural writes back straight away. MCP makes that easy because reading is just another tool, and the agent and the developer end up looking at the same facts.

MCP is awesome because it makes the boring plumbing legible. That leaves more room for the interesting decisions.

Every integration used to be a bespoke adapter. Each assistant, each tool and each CMS needed its own glue code, its own auth story and its own idea of what a request looks like.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) replaces that patchwork with one contract. A server exposes capabilities as named tools with typed inputs. A client discovers them and calls them. That is the whole idea, and it is a good one.

content.text:
The blog is built and running. The front page lists both posts, and both post pages render with no fallback errors.

**What I built**

- **Content model (via MCP):**
  - Three block element types in `Blocks`: `heroBlock`, `richTextBlock`, `imageBlock`.
  - A block grid data type, "Page Blocks", that allows those three blocks.
  - Two page types in `Pages`: `blogFrontPage` (a block grid plus the post list) and `blogPost` (title, summary, publish date, hero image, and a block grid body).
  - Templates for both page types, and `allowedTemplates`/`allowedDocumentTypes` wired up. The Site Root now allows Blog Front Page beneath it.
- **Content (via MCP):**
  - A "Blog" front page under WWW with the `/` domain, published. Its block grid holds a hero and an intro rich text block.
  - Two published posts, "Why MCP is awesome" and "Why MCP is awesome, part 2", each with a rich text, image and rich text body.
  - A "Blog" media folder with five Unsplash photos imported from `unsplash/`.
- **Razor (after restart):**
  - Block adapters in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/` (`heroBlock`, `richTextBlock`, `imageBlock`) that hand plain models to ViewComponents.
  - Four ViewComponents (`Hero`, `RichText`, `Image`, `PostList`) with their views, plus plain models in `Models/Blog/`.
  - `_Layout.cshtml` and the two page views. Images use `GetCropUrl`.
  - Tailwind and the Vue bundle built into `wwwroot/dist`. This needed `npm install` in `Umbraco.Bench.Frontend`.

**How to view it**

Umbraco is running in the background. Open https://localhost:44317/ (the HTTP port 41576 also answers).
- Front page: `/`
- Posts: `/why-mcp-is-awesome/` and `/why-mcp-is-awesome-part-2/`

**Choices I made**

- The post list is page-level Razor (`Children<BlogPost>()` into a PostList ViewComponent), not a block. The adapters can't see the page, so a list block would need a different design.
- I created the Block Grid data type myself because none existed. I guessed its config shape. Reading the schema back confirmed the three block types were applied.

**Not working or not verified**

- **Photo credits:** the image blocks carry photographer captions, but the hero photos (Conny Schneider, Alina Grubnyak, Christopher Gower) have no visible credit. I didn't add one.
- **Visual check:** I checked the HTML, not a screenshot. Every response was 200, with no fallback errors, the hero image URL present, and the CSS served.
- **uSync:** I didn't confirm that the schema changes exported to `uSync/`.
- **Process slip:** I ran a foreground `dotnet build` while the background `dotnet run` was still building. That caused one failed start. I re-ran the build sequentially, and it succeeded with 0 warnings after fixing two nullable warnings.
